summary:
Same-sex relations are legal in Liechtenstein, and the country's anti-discrimination framework prohibits discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation. Gender identity, gender expression and sex characteristics are not covered by any anti-discrimination statute in force. No procedure exists for changing a legal gender marker in official documents, and no law restricts access to sex-segregated facilities. Medical interventions on the genitals of intersex children are not prohibited by law.

Civil marriage and joint adoption have been available to same-sex couples since January 2025. The Landtag's motion of September 2022, 'Motion zur Öffnung der Ehe für alle', sought to open civil marriage regardless of gender and sexual orientation and to remove the remaining legal differences, noting that registered partnerships were perceived as a second-class marriage. The motion also recorded that Prince Hans-Adam II had stated in 2021 that he had nothing against marriage equality other than adoption.

Official hostility is a live factor. In his New Year interview of January 2016 Prince Hans-Adam II called rainbow families 'irresponsible', asserted that children have 'a right to a normal family', and suggested that Liechtenstein could 'ignore' an adverse ruling of the European Court of Human Rights; the local LGBT organisation Flay responded that it was 'choqué' and the Freie Liste called the remarks contrary to the Constitution and the European Convention on Human Rights. The state religion is Roman Catholicism, and the archbishop publicly opposed marriage equality.

Entry falls under the common border-free travel zone operated with Switzerland and Austria, and no source reports friction at that border for trans travellers. There is no documented pattern of anti-trans violence in the country. Liechtenstein is very small, has very low crime, and is closely integrated with both neighbouring states; the first Pride was held in 2022.
tangentialFactors:
Local commentary from 2012 describes a population of roughly 35,000 with no organised gay scene, with friendship networks serving that function, and reports 'few organised enemies... no religious extremists, no right-wing skinheads, no political rogues demanding homophobic laws', with gay people living comfortably and with little interference. The account is dated and written before the marriage-equality debate and the 2016 remarks of the head of state, so it describes the social climate rather than the present legal position.

The trajectory of the small European states on LGBT equality has been treated comparatively in the press; a Reuters feature covering Liechtenstein among them could not be retrieved at research time (HTTP 401), so its specific content is unavailable.
localsOnly:
The gaps in Liechtenstein's anti-discrimination coverage bind residents, employers and public bodies rather than travellers: a trans resident who is dismissed, refused service or harassed on grounds of gender identity, gender expression or sex characteristics has no statutory anti-discrimination claim, while discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation is prohibited.

The absence of any procedure for changing a legal gender marker means residents must continue to present documents carrying their original marker. Absence of a statutory ban on interventions on intersex children is a matter of domestic healthcare regulation.

Opposition to same-sex marriage and adoption has come from the head of state and from the Catholic hierarchy, the state religion. Public debate over the issue is conducted openly, and the first Pride was held in 2022.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the inventory documents how border officers, document checks or security screening treat a traveller whose presentation does not match the marker in their passport; the absence of reported friction at the Swiss and Austrian borders is an absence of evidence, not a sourced assurance.

The inventory contains no information on legal gender recognition in neighbouring Switzerland or Austria, nor on how a Liechtenstein-issued document without a marker change would be read by either state.

Access to gender-affirming healthcare, its cost, waiting times and the availability of prescribing clinicians, is not sourced here; nor is any provision on name change independent of a gender marker change.

The Reuters feature on small European states and LGBT equality returned HTTP 401 at research time, so its claims about Liechtenstein could not be verified.
